title: Learning Many-Body Hamiltonians Using a Local Probe
authors: Suying Liu, Zitai Xu, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Xiaodi Wu, Yu-Xin Wang, Zhi-Yuan Wei
abstract: Hamiltonian learning provides a systematic framework for reconstructing unknown quantum dynamics. However, existing protocols typically assume direct measurement access to the entire system. With fast single-qubit control and a connected reference backbone, we show that a single measurable qubit suffices to learn all $O(N)$ independent parameters of a bounded-degree two-body Hamiltonian on $N$ qubits at the Heisenberg limit. Crucially, our protocol uses robust SWAP gates synthesized by quantum signal processing, enabling coherent transfer of states evolving under distant Hamiltonian parameters to the measurable qubit. This transfer requires no prior calibration of the Hamiltonian parameters of the intermediate links. A parallel learning architecture achieves total query time $\widetilde{O}(N)$ for an $N$-qubit chain, while retaining Heisenberg-limited precision scaling. On the chain, these scalings match the fundamental precision and information-propagation lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. The framework further extends to arbitrary bounded-degree interaction graphs. Our results establish a scalable route to learning an extensive number of many-body Hamiltonian parameters through only a local measurement interface.
summary: This paper presents a novel protocol to learn the parameters of an unknown many-body Hamiltonian using measurements restricted to a single local qubit. By employing parallel phase encoding and robust quantum information transfer techniques, the authors achieve Heisenberg-limited precision scaling. This establishes a scalable route for characterizing complex quantum dynamics with minimal measurement access.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of reconstructing unknown many-body Hamiltonians by measuring only a single, local qubit.
main_result: It demonstrates that a single measurable qubit is sufficient to learn all $O(N)$ parameters of a bounded-degree two-body Hamiltonian on $N$ qubits at the Heisenberg limit.
method: The protocol combines parallel phase encoding with robust information transfer, utilizing synthesized SWAP gates to move state information from distant qubits to the local probe.
model_or_system: The system is an $N$-qubit chain or general graph evolving under an unknown nearest-neighbor two-body Hamiltonian. Control is restricted to fast single-qubit operations and measurement on one 'bright qubit'.
key_observables: The primary observables are the expectation values of Pauli operators ($\langle X angle_t, \langle Y angle_t, \langle Z angle_t$) measured on the local probe qubit.
important_parameters: The scaling is characterized by achieving Heisenberg-limited precision ($\epsilon$) and a total query time of $e^{O(N)}$ for the chain, matching fundamental lower bounds.
main_assumptions: Assumes fast single-qubit control and the existence of a connected reference backbone interaction to facilitate information propagation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the protocol overview, showing initialization, parallel encoding of unknown parameters into phases, and sequential readout at the bright qubit, including details on constructing robust SWAP operations.
paper_structure: The paper develops the protocol by first establishing the general framework for local-probe Hamiltonian learning, then detailing the specific implementation for the 1D chain model, and finally analyzing the complexity scaling for arbitrary bounded-degree interaction graphs using graph theory techniques.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, scalable measurement protocol that drastically reduces the experimental overhead required to characterize complex quantum dynamics, which is crucial for designing and benchmarking quantum hardware.

Repeatedly resetting the bright qubit and applying robust SWAPs prepares the register approximately in the all-zero state. The unknown Hamiltonian parameters are then encoded in parallel into quantum states distributed across the system. Alternating SWAP layers transport this information back toward the bright qubit, where the encoded states are read out sequentially. (b) The SWAP operations are constructed directly from the unknown interactions using quantum signal processing.
